whether it is held in canada. the important thing is that it happens before 12 december. canada is important for a variety of reasons and i shall be telegraphic in saying this because mr vitorino and mr schröder have already outlined some of those. the links that we have are important for cultural and historical reasons. i was hoping that the summit would nurture further exchanges between young people so that we can retain those existing links and build upon them for the future. the eu and canada are natural partners on the world stage. we both value, in a way that some other countries do not, the multilateral institutions of the world and we value the international rule of law. much is to be gained by working with our canadian partners on issues as diverse as the implementation of the kyoto protocol, the jurisdiction of the international court of justice, and the doha trade negotiations. again, as the commissioner rightly outlined, our economic and trade relations are good. importantly, they are good in a two-way sense: it is not a one-way trading relationship. canada's willingness to reach an agreement on trade in wine and spirits demonstrates the goodwill that characterises our relationship with the canadians. finally, on justice and home affairs, we have a common approach to issues as diverse as terrorism, migration, asylum and border controls, as well as issues of the integration of migrants. i hope - and i address this to commissioner vitorino - that we can find a solution to canada's desire to have a longer visa period for canadian citizens visiting the eu. in conclusion, i share the commission's view about the eu's relationship with canada. i hope that this house will join with the european commission in stressing to the council the importance of the summit going ahead in some shape or form.
madam president, i share the views expressed by my colleague, mr martin. we would be forgiven for thinking over these last months that europe has only one transatlantic relationship, so often do we use that term to describe the link between our union and the united states of america. the canadian prime minister, pierre trudeau, once said that living next to america was like 'sleeping with an elephant'. even its smallest movements were likely to keep you awake at night. europe's own sensitivity to the movements of the current american elephant can all too easily overshadow our relations with its northern neighbour. the eu-canada summit is a chance to renew this relationship. the european union and canada have a long history of productive cooperation to build on. we share the same views on the best strategy for defeating international terrorism and international organised crime. we are common supporters of nato, the un and the icc. we share a strong commitment to third world development assistance and environmental protection. both the eu and canada have ratified the kyoto protocols, and led the call for others to do so. the ottawa land mines convention expresses our joint abhorrence of these weapons and our determination to act. there was a time when canada sought actively bilateral trading links with europe as a way of reducing its dependence on trade with the united states. it would be facile to see nafta as canada's surrender to economic destiny. canadians continue to invest significantly in europe: almost eur 65 billion last year. in return, we provide over a quarter of foreign investment in canada. we take almost 20% of canada's service-related exports. the commission's strategy document dwells rightly on the good will which exists between us, but identifies rightly that very little positive action flows from it. we must deliver such action. high level meetings between canada and the eu have too often lacked clear objectives. this summit should re-launch our relations on much more proactive terms. the presidency has recognised this, in making the negotiation of an ambitious new accord one of the priorities of its tenure. for this reason, it is extraordinary that the president-in-office of the council has chosen not to accompany his delegation. i have been told by canadian diplomats this evening that mr berlusconi's tactless decision has led canada to consider cancelling the summit altogether, or to reschedule it for a european venue earlier in december. given the importance of this summit and its established place in europe's diplomatic calendar, mr berlusconi has shown an unacceptable willingness to offend our friends in ottawa. for the second time in as many weeks he has embarrassed the union, and in this case offended a valuable ally. the eldr urges strongly that the summit goes ahead in december as planned, preferably in canada, and in europe only as a last resort. even in mr berlusconi's absence, this summit must deliver an agreement that takes away regulatory barriers to closer trade and investment. given the importance of our large store of common north atlantic values, this summit should assert that canada and the eu will henceforth cooperate proactively in foreign and security policy and on environmental questions. this means aligning our positions before major international meetings. the summit must also produce concrete proposals for a steering group to assess the future management of our relationship. we need more formal meetings at official and expert level, and a much more focused relationship. as soon as a constitutional settlement is achieved, the 1976 framework agreement with canada should be updated. in conclusion, it is time to equip our other transatlantic relationship for the new century.
mr president, on a point of order, i want to report to parliament that at the september part-session this parliament passed a report on the lloyd's petitions, setting a deadline of 15 november for the commission to provide information to parliament about its regulation of lloyd's of london between 1978 and 2001. i have to report that by 15 november no such communication had been received from the commission. as rapporteur, i still am not aware of anything having been received by parliament, although i am assured by mr bolkestein's services that his letter is in the post. i hope that will be received in due course, but the deadline was not respected. i shall raise this matter in writing, but i just wanted to put it on record.
- the agenda calls for a joint debate on three community action programmes:- report (a5-0384/2003) by mr sacrédeus, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, on the proposal for a council decision establishing a community action programme for bodies promoting mutual understanding between the european union and certain non-industrialised regions of the world (com (2003) 280 - c5-0350/2003 - 2003/0110cns)) - report (a5-0368/2003) by mrs rühle, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a council decision establishing a community action programme for the promotion of european citizenship (civil participation) (com (2003) 276 - c5-021/03 - c6-021/2003 - c6-011/2003 - c6-039/2003 - c06-0523/2003 - c06-0523/2003 - c06-0523/2003 - c06-0523/2003 - c06-0523/2003 - c06-0523/2003 - c06-0523/2003 - c06-0523/03 - c07-05-05/2003 - c07-05-05-05-039 - c07-05-05-09-09-03) - report by mrs c010/05-05-06-09
commission - mr president, since this is a joint debate, the bad news is that i will have to speak for quite a long time, but the good news is that i will be as quick as possible, while not forgetting to answer the detailed questions that have been raised by members in the course of their work, which i know reflect the hard and intense work that they have done. as the house is aware, the three european institutions worked together to secure a new financial regulation in 2002 which came into force on 1 january 2003. the regulation provides, among other things, a clear framework for the grants with which we support a large number of european organisations in the context of the dialogue with european citizens. it also states that every financial decision should be based on a legal basis to ensure its justification. this requirement is particularly relevant for grants which were financed from lines whose position in the budget structure - the so-called part a of the budget - meant that they could be treated as administrative expenditure and, therefore, be carried out without a clear legal basis. the change in the budget structure introduced in the new financial regulation has ended this assimilation to administrative expenditure, which means that a legal basis is now required for these grants. this new obligation led the commission to present, in may 2003, seven proposals for new legal bases. these were accompanied by a communication by mrs schreyer which highlighted the common context and presented identical solutions to common problems. the commission welcomes this report by mr sacrédeus and is pleased that the drafters and parliament have given priority to this commission proposal. with the parliament's opinion, it should now be possible for the decision to enter into force in 2004 and for it to be followed by a call for proposals to select the beneficiaries who will be awarded grants for the following year. the objective agreed between parliament and the council at the conciliation meeting on 16 july was the entry into force in 2004 of legal bases for grants not covered by this coverage. the legal basis presented today, together with the six other proposals on grants, is important because it is a direct consequence of the innovations on grants under the new financial regulation and is firmly rooted in the fundamental principles of transparency and equal treatment of potential beneficiaries. most of the amendments proposed in parliament's resolution can be accepted by the commission and are in line with the spirit of the commission's proposal. however, the commission considers that it would be appropriate to limit the amount of the subsidies to 70% of the eligible costs, instead of 80%. similarly, the commission is of the opinion that a degressivity rate of 10% per year is preferable to 2.5%. we believe that these two requirements are safeguards that will help to ensure sustainability and encourage beneficiaries to be active in seeking other sources of complementary income. one point worth mentioning is the need to ensure consistency between the proposal for a council decision and the budget. in the preliminary draft budget, the commission proposed a budget line to consolidate the amounts which were distributed over four lines in chapter a 30 of the 2003 budget. the future legal basis for this single line, as required by the new financial regulation, is the proposal for a decision which is being presented to the house today. this decision provides for the selection of beneficiaries following a call for proposals, in accordance with the principles of transparency and equal treatment. at first reading parliament replaced the single line with five lines. the title of each line is the name of an institute. there is a clear incompatibility between the future legal basis and such a division of the budget line. the commission hopes that the adopted budget will be in line with the proposal of the apb, thus allowing us to implement the proposal and the appropriations in full compliance with community law, as required by the new financial regulation adopted by this house and the council. i now turn to mrs rühle's report on the proposal for an action programme to promote active european citizenship. i thank mrs rühle for recognising the urgency of this matter and for ensuring that it was swiftly adopted by the committee on civil liberties and human rights, justice and home affairs, which proved to be very useful. the commission proposal to this house aims to ensure a smooth transition from the old system to the new arrangements and continuity in the activities concerned. we have endeavoured to produce a text which, to a large extent, extends the 2003 implementation procedures while incorporating the requirements of the new financial regulation in terms of sound financial management of public funds. this proposed legal basis should therefore be considered as a technical adjustment. nevertheless, there is a strong temptation, understandably, to seize the opportunity to add innovations and suggest improvements. parliament, as usual, is extremely efficient with this creativity. however, this can be risky - particularly if such additions jeopardise the subsequent adoption of the proposal by the council. the commission proposal has therefore been formulated in a way which we consider moderate, its main objective being to continue what has already been achieved and to provide a legal structure which is consistent with the new financial regulation. i therefore urge the honourable members not to depart too far from the commission's proposals and to do everything possible to ensure that this legal basis is adopted as soon as possible. furthermore, as regards the legal basis for active european citizenship, the room for manoeuvre is even more limited since unanimity is required within the council. all the possibilities for compromise must be explored if we are to succeed in completing this procedure as soon as possible. in fact, as from 1 january 2004, in the absence of this legal basis, we simply would no longer be able to provide financial support to all organisations actively involved in promoting european citizenship. we would regret it bitterly, as would undoubtedly parliament. i shall now explain the commission's position on the amendments to mrs rühle's report. the commission can fully accept amendments nos 1, 4, 7, 9, 11, 12, 15, 16, 13 and 31, which provide useful clarifications to the text. while recalling the need to apply the new financial regulation, the commission does not object to amendment 45 on the simplification of administrative procedures. the commission will of course oblige those who have received european grants to make adequate publicity. while we fully share the parliament's view on this matter, as is shown in amendment no 48, we believe that it would be more appropriate to include this obligation in the agreements to be signed with the beneficiaries. the same applies to amendment no 49 on the dissemination and availability of results. the commission agrees with amendment 47, which stresses the need for regular exchanges of views with beneficiaries. the commission can accept amendment no 25 in part. since the amendment does not change the substance of the commission's proposal, we can accept the proposal to specify that the budgetary appropriations planned for the period after 2006 are subject to an agreement by the budgetary authority on the financial perspective beyond 2006. however, the commission is prepared to accept the same duration for the seven proposals in the package until 2006 if this can help to find a compromise for all the proposals with a view to their adoption in time for the implementation of the budget in 2004. since this proposal must be considered in conjunction with the other proposals in the package, the amendments on the pre-allocation of appropriations and the possibility of establishing an executive agency must also be dealt with in a broader context. in the same amendment, the commission cannot accept the reference to the total amount allocated to the programme as this aspect is not in accordance with the legislative procedures provided for in the consultation procedure. the commission can also accept amendment no 28 in part. we have no objection to sending reports on the implementation of the programme, but we cannot accept to transfer the content of the annex to article 8 (a), which would not correspond to the usual format of legal texts. the same applies to amendments nos 20, 21, 22, 29 and 30, which the commission rejects. the commission understands parliament's view on the issue of focusing on the potential enlargement of the scope and objectives of this proposal. however, we intend to ensure the continuity of activities which the commission has already supported in the past, so we have to reject amendments nos 14, 40, 41, 42 and 43 in order to reach a unanimous position on our proposal in the council. amendments nos 6 and 33 concerning the european movement are rejected, as are amendments nos 32, 34, 35, 36 and 37, which add new organisations to the list of beneficiaries. in order to ensure the continuity of the funding currently allocated, the commission considers it not appropriate to start a discussion on the list of organisations in part 1. in accordance with the financial regulation, we intend to launch a call for proposals which will be open to all organisations active in this field. however, in order to facilitate the transition from the system of pre-allocation to the system of calls for proposals and taking into account the time remaining before the programme enters into force, we believe that it would be more appropriate to apply the pre-allocation model in 2004 and to publish an open call for proposals from 2005 onwards. this would be a reasonable compromise since it would be technically impossible, under the procedures laid down in the financial regulation, to launch a call for proposals after the adoption of this legal basis which would still allow funding from the beginning of 2004. the commission can therefore accept in principle the application of a system of advance allocation of appropriations. however, we believe that this approach should be limited to 2004 and that the operating rules should be set out in the annex rather than in the programme text. therefore, for technical reasons, the commission cannot accept the part of amendment no 23 relating to group 1. the part of the amendment relating to group 2 and aimed at incorporating organisations with a different perspective on the union's policies is considered to be rather superfluous and we cannot therefore accept it. the last part of the amendment is not in line with the usual format of legal texts and is also rejected. as regards the possible involvement of an executive agency in the management of part of the programme, in particular as regards the management of the many projects in the twinning part of the programme, the commission stresses that such an approach is in accordance with article 55 of the financial regulation applicable to the general budget of the european communities. in fact, the commission is considering the establishment of such an executive agency in the fields of education and culture. depending on the conclusions of a cost-benefit study currently being prepared by an external consultant, the commission could propose that such an agency be partly involved in the management of this programme. before taking a final decision, the commission will submit this proposal to the council's executive agency committee. therefore, the commission is not in a position at this time to accept amendment no 46. the commission rejects amendments nos 2, 8, 10, 17, 19, 24 and 50, which it considers superfluous because the issues they address are already sufficiently detailed in the existing text or covered by other texts. the reference to full employment in amendment 3 is rejected as being too ambitious. amendment 5, which refers to the draft constitution, is premature since it can still be amended. we believe that the proposal to carry out regular evaluations of the organisations listed in part 1, mentioned in amendment no 38, would be far too burdensome to implement since these organisations are listed as beneficiaries for the entire duration of the programme. any amendment to the list would therefore require a new council decision. amendment no 39 is unacceptable because it goes against the very essence of the action programme which aims to encourage european networks. amendment no 40 on the media is also rejected because it may undermine the demands of grassroots organisations. the commission rejects amendment no 44, which represents an unacceptable interference with the commission's implementing powers. the information of national parliaments, as suggested in amendment 27, is not appropriate and the commission considers that any evaluation of the programme should be based on a two-year reference period and therefore rejects amendment 26. amendment no 51, which was tabled after the adoption of mrs rühle's report in committee, is unacceptable to the commission as it does not guarantee the implementation of the programmes before the adoption of the legal basis. in conclusion, as regards this particular reply, the commission can accept 14 of the 51 amendments tabled by parliament in full, 2 in part and rejects 35. i call on the house to do all it can to ensure that the support given by the european union to the creation of european citizenship is not aborted. if we want the system to be back on track by early 2004, an agreement at this stage of the procedure will be decisive and i know that honourable members are fully aware of this. i thank the house for its attention. i have a few more points to address briefly before concluding. they concern the decision of the parliament and the council establishing a community programme for the promotion of organisations active at european level in the field of equality between women and men. i would first like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs kratsa-tsagaropoulou, and the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities on their work and achievements on this dossier, which have been considerable in every respect. i am pleased that progress has already been made in the council and parliament on this basic piece of legislation which is designed to provide a legal basis for the continuation of financial support to organisations active at european level in the promotion of gender equality. i welcome most of the 20 amendments to the report by mrs kratsa-tsagaropoulou, adopted on 3 november 2003 in the committee on women's rights, because they bring more precision and clarity to this basic legislative text. however, the commission opposes certain amendments concerning aspects relating to the duration of the programme and its evaluation. the commission proposed a two-year period - 2004 and 2005 - because it will include this topic in the general reflections on the future of the equality strategy after 2005. the commission cannot therefore accept the extension of the duration of the programme until 2008, as proposed in amendment 8. the commission therefore cannot accept amendments 6 and 7 on degressivity, amendment 9 on the increase in the financial envelope, or amendment 10 on the agreement of the budgetary authority beyond 2006. as regards the commission's evaluation of the programme, the financial regulation provides the necessary sound framework. amendment no 11, which suggests that this evaluation be based on an external report, is therefore unnecessary and seems disproportionate to the small amounts involved in this programme and its duration. the commission rejects amendment no 19 because it considers that it is better to keep the themes at a general rather than a specific level. finally, the commission cannot accept amendment 20 because it would undermine the commission's role in implementing the programme. the adoption of this basic legislative text as soon as possible is very important in order not to disrupt the community's financial support to these organisations, in particular the european women's lobby. in summary, the commission can accept amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18 and reject amendments nos 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 19 and 20 for the reasons i have just set out. i thank the house for its patience with me, who made a rather long speech.

in writing. - (pt) we rejected this attempt to impose a pseudo-constitutional process in order to legitimise the convention document. we do not agree with the support expressed for the financial provisions contained in it. these provisions are intended to introduce a major change in substance from the existing treaty by including the financial perspective and the budgetary discharge in the 'constitution'. in other words, they intend to transform the current interinstitutional agreement and 'constitutionalise' the financial perspective, by imposing a greater obstacle to its revision or amendment and by making the approval of the annual budget conditional on the upper limit of the financial perspective, as is clear from the reading of articles 52 (5) and 54 (3) and the provisions of article iii-308. we have always defended a financial perspective which guarantees the principle of economic and social cohesion in an enlarged eu, and we cannot forget that we now have the smallest budget since 1987 in relative terms, less than 1% of community gnp, which requires a revision of the financial perspective. as for the amendment relating to the referendum on the igc results, i would like to say that our vote in favour of the referendum is unambiguous: it clearly indicates that we are opposed to a european referendum or a referendum to be held on the same day as the european elections and that we demand respect for the constitutional rules of the member states.
mr president, i am sorry that it is commissioner kinnock who has to be here this afternoon to take this criticism on the chin, because i in no way regard him as personally responsible for the situation in which we find ourselves. i shall put some simple questions to which we all know the answers and on which we are all agreed. is the average european citizen in need of extra information about the european union? yes. is information needed in the member states and locally rather than in brussels? yes. do the info-points help meet that need? yes. is next year, with enlargement, with the new constitution, with elections, a year when the information will be more necessary than usual? yes. has the commission got its organisation and priorities right on information policy? that is questionable. of course expenditure must meet legal requirements and if a legal base is necessary then it must be found. we employ lawyers precisely to check on those points in good time, advise if there is a problem and indicate a solution. we knew about the problem in january and the commission's solution was to send the info-points a letter at the end of september. that really is not good enough. after all, the amount of expenditure is pretty minimal. it has been allocated over a good many years. if the commission doubts the need for info-points and the more effective information programme, let me draw attention to statistics in recent polls. 90% of spaniards have never heard of the convention. 31% of germans have never heard of the commission and 25% of britons do not even know that the united kingdom is a member of the european union but 7% of them think that america is! the english language is rich in expressions. let me try and find some that fit this situation. the tail is wagging the dog. the commission appears to be unable to see the wood for the trees. experts should be on tap, not on top. i could carry on with vulgar expressions about breweries and organising parties in them. there is not a major legal difficulty here, it is a technical problem. if the commission had clear and accepted priorities and could see the wood for the trees, we would not be having this debate this afternoon. i welcome commissioner kinnock's statement, but he knows as well as we do that it has come far too late and it really should not have been necessary. sadly, this is another own goal by the commission. i hope that the letter that will be sent to the info-points will contain an apology.
mr president, this debate comes at a very timely moment in the history of indonesia, given the very grave situation in the province of aceh. the decision by the indonesian authorities to extend martial law and carry out a military crackdown is deeply regrettable, and there has been very heavy-handed military action. an estimated 45 000 troops have been sent into the province against 5000 rebels. as ever in these situations, it is the civilian population which is paying the price, with reports of disruption to food supplies, infrastructure and schools being destroyed. tens of thousands of civilians are reportedly displaced. these are only estimates, of course, because the indonesian authorities are not allowing observers in to monitor the situation. this has to stop. there is no point in the indonesian government complaining when the international community, the united states, the eu and japan, draft a resolution expressing their concern if they in turn are not prepared to allow international monitors in and are not prepared to allow humanitarian organisations into their country to bring assistance to the civilian population. our joint resolution makes a series of demands on the indonesian government and i hope very much that it is listening and that it will heed those concerns. it is vital to get both parties back to the negotiating table as quickly as possible. time and time again we hear people telling us that military action is the answer, that it will be a quick military action and that once it is over everything will be sorted out. we have heard this so often, but often been disappointed. so often we have seen a high price paid in human lives. so both sides, the gam and the indonesian government, must get back to the negotiating table, stop the fighting and resume the talking. i am grateful to the commission for what it is already doing as regards indonesia, particularly commissioner patten, who has always taken up issues about aceh when we have asked him to do so. i hope the council and the commission will now do everything possible to assist indonesia in getting back to the negotiating table with gam and get those talks started as soon as possible. this is a matter of some urgency and i am very grateful to colleagues in this parliament for agreeing to have today's debate and for supporting this resolution.
mr president, for me this is not a debate on the rights and wrongs of those in aceh who campaign for independence, nor is it a criticism of indonesia's right to intervene to secure law and order, so long, of course, as that country does not permit human rights abuses to be committed by any of its forces. it is a debate about the escalating humanitarian crisis. as we know, most of aceh's 4.2 million people live outside the two main towns. for them food, water, electricity and communications have been disrupted. healthcare and education have become impossible. five hundred schools have been burnt down, thousands of people have fled from their homes and governor puteh has said that unemployment and poverty are now at alarming rates. we worry about human rights and i raise two issues. one is the fact that 77 community heads have been replaced by military personnel and the second is that active in aceh are people like major general damiri, brigadier general suratman and others who have been convicted of crimes against humanity in east timor. they are on duty in aceh. kofi annan has appealed to indonesia to ensure access to humanitarian aid and human rights organisations. he is right. the obstacles to this are in presidential decree 43/2003, which states that international and local ngos are not allowed to conduct activities contrary to the objectives of the military emergency conditions. that is a catch-all provision that is exacerbating the humanitarian crisis. it is not acceptable that all aid has to be rooted through the indonesian authorities, nor that ngos are restricted to banda aceh. finally, we call on indonesia to investigate with urgency the disappearance of the human rights defender abdussalam deli, and the killing of his colleague, raja ismail. i hope the commission and the council will assist us in these aims.

counsel. - (it) mr president, mr president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the european parliament for the opportunity it has given me to present to you the main topics which will be discussed at the next european council on the agenda in brussels on 12 and 13 december. this summit, which will close the six-month period of the italian presidency, is an extremely important date for us, not only for the major themes that will be discussed, but also for the decisions that will be adopted there, decisions that will mark the course of the future work of the union on some of the most important subjects on the european agenda. the european summit - as you know - will have to leave enough room for the work of the intergovernmental conference, which will meet, for its final phase, at the level of the heads of state or government, assisted by their respective foreign ministers. given the importance of the subject, i would like to start by giving an update on the state of the igc's work, and then return to the preparations for the next european summit. with the italian presidency's six-month term coming to an end, i am pleased to inform you of the developments in the wake of the naples conclave. i would like to begin by reaffirming that the overall position of the italian presidency remains the one my government has repeatedly expressed in parliament and in the igc. in accordance with this position, the overall proposal presented reflects the intention to respect the draft treaty submitted to us by the convention, by limiting itself to proposing clarifications or adaptations to the draft convention in the light of the comments made by the member states, the european parliament and the commission. i think i can say that many of the presidency's proposals have been widely appreciated, which has enabled us to bring the positions of the member states closer together while respecting the overall balance of the draft convention. in addition to the significant progress made on a few specific issues, it was clearly perceived that some remaining differences on specific provisions could be resolved if agreement was reached on the future institutional framework of the union. the most significant objections remain in this area, particularly as regards the calculation of the qualified majority in the council and the composition of the commission. a detailed analysis of the results of the conclave shows that progress has been made on the following points of our package of proposals: the inclusion of a reference to equality between women and men and the protection of persons belonging to minorities in the provision on the values of the union; the reaffirmation of the primacy of union law; the requirement to submit the acts of the european council to judicial review in so far as the latter is defined by the constitutional treaty as an institution of the union. there were also signs of convergence in the highly sensitive area of justice and home affairs. in this area, the introduction of qualified majority voting will have to take account of the specificities of certain national legal systems and provide for protection mechanisms. the various proposals made by the presidency on specific policies in the third part of the draft constitutional treaty were discussed in depth. in several cases, the positions of the member states continue to differ on the basis of known lines of divergence. however, it seems very clear that various critical remarks made in this context will dissipate once agreement is reached on the main thematic issues of the constitutional negotiations. among the issues that will need further exploration are: the persistent divergences between countries that do not want to make concessions on the abolition of unanimity on matters such as foreign policy, taxation and social security and those member states that, on the other hand, consider the gradual introduction of qualified majority voting in these areas as an essential element of the future constitutional treaty; the commission is also aware of the numerous (often divergent) requests from member states for amendments to the provisions on the budget, the multiannual financial framework, own resources and economic governance. here the presidency aims to preserve as far as possible the interinstitutional balances and the voting rules proposed by the convention. the idea of a simplified revision procedure for title iii of part iii of the constitutional treaty continues to meet with resistance, while greater convergence seems to be emerging on the 'bridge clause' on the basis of formulas which also involve national parliaments. on all these issues, the presidency reserved the right to propose new ideas during the last igc sessions. the conclave also made significant progress on the definition of esdp in the future constitutional treaty. it was possible to achieve a new wording of article i-40 (7) on the mutual assistance clause, the description of structured cooperation in article iii-213 and, above all, the presentation of a protocol containing the criteria for participation in this cooperation. this package of texts will be reviewed at the igc ministerial meeting on 8 december. however, the exchange of views during the conclave revealed increasing elements of convergence in this sensitive thematic area. the debate on the institutional framework of the future union confirmed that this is the most sensitive area of the whole negotiation. the conclave proved useful in overcoming some points of disagreement and above all in promoting a more peaceful and constructive confrontation. the main points of the discussion can be summarised as follows. the request by some member states to raise the minimum threshold for national members of the european parliament was welcomed, provided that the total number of seats did not increase. on the subject of the presidency of council configurations, there is a convergence in the convention's guidelines, even if some member states remain perplexed about the collegial presidencies, which they would prefer to have elected representatives. the italian presidency reserved the right to consider further adaptations on this subject. the solution that could be reached would be that of three member states holding the presidency for 18 months. the detailed arrangements for implementing these solutions could be decided by the european council, rather than being governed by a specific protocol. the reactions to the presidency's proposals on the union minister for foreign affairs - aimed at clarifying certain aspects of the operation of the 'double-hat' formula in keeping with the spirit of the draft convention - have confirmed that the system we have chosen is the only viable one. our suggestions tend to overcome both the criticisms of those who fear that the new institutional figure will become a trojan horse for the council within the commission, weakening its powers in external relations, and those of the member states who would like to remove the minister from the constraints of the commission's collegial nature by emphasizing his role as the council's representative. the middle way we have indicated seems to be the only one capable of securing a final compromise, even if two important questions remain to be resolved: the persistent opposition of some countries to entrusting the foreign minister with the presidency of the council for external relations, and the request of other states not to appoint the new institutional figure as "minister" but more modestly as "representative", with an obvious backward step - not only symbolic - in relation to the draft convention. during the long debate on the composition of the commission after 2009, some of the positions and arguments already known were put forward again. in the further negotiations, it will be necessary to reconcile the supporters of a small, agile, efficient commission unhampered by intergovernmental constraints with the advocates of a commission representative of all national cultures and sensibilities and, therefore, composed of one commissioner with a voting right per member state. the proposals on the table will have to be analysed in a long-term perspective and in the light of the institutional requirements of a union which, in 10-15 years' time, is likely to have an even wider composition and will therefore have to be equipped with adequate decision-making capacities that are easily understood by the citizens. the confrontation on the question of calculating the qualified majority in the council has brought even more clearly to light the range of positions at stake: some states defend the nice system valiantly, others consider the transition to the double majority to be unavoidable. among the latter, several countries would prefer a fully symmetrical double majority - i.e. 50% or even 60% of both the member states and the population of the union. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. in this respect, and to repeat what i have said previously, i stress the need to look at the various proposals in a long-term perspective beyond 2009. the igc ministerial session on 8 december and the bilateral meetings which the presidency will intensify in the coming weeks will therefore have to focus mainly on institutional issues in order to complete in the best possible way the preparations for the final meeting of the conference, at the level of heads of state or government, which will open on 12 december 2003. the success or failure of the constitutional negotiations will very likely determine the evolution of the integration process in the coming years and the ability of europe to play an influential role on the international scene in a context of major political and economic challenges. for this reason, and in view of the importance of the issue, the approach to the constitutional negotiations will have to be characterised by a good degree of flexibility on the part of all the actors called upon to lay the foundations of the union of the 21st century. in respect of the principle of equal dignity of all member states - which was also recognised at the conclave of naples - it is necessary to abandon particularism and to abandon the logic of 'just return' whereby, for each concession, an equal benefit is sought. this is an approach which runs counter to the very concept of european integration and which, if systematically applied, risks undermining the very foundations of the union. although fairness is an essential condition for any constitutional agreement, no one can now stop the current evolution of the integration process. those who want to move in this direction will be called upon to assume their responsibilities towards their european partners, towards their fellow citizens and towards the history of the integration process. political systems are the result of dialogue and action by men: men are entirely responsible for this dialogue and action. we must now know that the approval of the new constitution will be "a success for all or a failure for the union". there is no longer any substantial difference between the national interest and the european interest. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to focus briefly on some of the issues that will be discussed by the european council. as regards economic issues, and in particular the resumption of sustainable economic growth, the european council will be the culmination of the long work carried out since the thessaloniki european council and further developed by the heads of state or government at the summit last october. the european council in december will be called upon to give final approval to the growth initiative already endorsed by the ecofin council on 25 november, by adopting concrete decisions which can substantially contribute to improving the competitiveness of the european economic system and to developing the union's growth potential to the full, by promoting a higher level of investment in physical capital and in the development of human capital. in this area, the main objective will be to create a policy catalyst, by identifying a series of projects that can be started within the short period of two or three years, to provide a decisive acceleration in the creation of infrastructure and the implementation of more advanced research projects, so as to facilitate the mobilisation of the essential resources of the european investment bank and the private sector. moreover, from a different and more general point of view, but still in the context of strengthening the cohesion of the internal market and the recovery of growth, the italian presidency is keen that the european council endorse the agreement of the transport council on the commission's proposal for the revision of the ten networks - which, i would remind you, is the 'backbone' of the initiatives to complete the infrastructure network of enlarged europe - also in the light of the recent decisions to increase community contributions from 10 to 20% for projects on cross-border sections. let us now turn to the themes linked to the lisbon agenda, in particular those aspects of structural reforms, on which the next spring european council will have to devote its energy. i would remind you that the member states of the union, whose efforts in this area have been consistent, will now have a major opportunity to engage in open dialogue during the extraordinary meeting of the trilateral social summit, which will be a very important occasion to renew the european union's commitment to implementing the european employment strategy. the social summit will be the occasion for a first review of the results of the work of the working party on employment led by wim kok, and also for a discussion on the growth initiative, particularly with regard to its effects on employment. on this basis, the social summit participants will be able to reflect more deeply on the links between employment growth and productivity growth, as highlighted by the wim kok working group, by assessing in particular the impact, also in terms of jobs, of policies aimed at improving the competitiveness of the economic system through the enhancement of human capital and the flexibility of european socioeconomic systems. the results of this summit - which mr berlusconi will report to the european council - will naturally also feed into the council's discussion. the european council will also provide an opportunity to take stock of the situation on certain important issues related to the construction of a common area of freedom, security and justice, in particular with regard to european immigration strategies, in the light of the indications emerging from the recent summits in brussels in october and thessaloniki in june. the heads of state or government will first have to take note of the agreements reached by the justice and home affairs council on 27 and 28 november on the main elements of a european border management agency, on a programme of measures specifically devoted to immigration by sea and on the introduction of biometric data in visas and residence permits. these are initiatives already discussed at the october summit and will now be rapidly implemented and, in some cases, further developed by the formal adoption of the relevant legislative acts. in this connection, i would like to stress that the european parliament will also have to express its opinion on the regulations concerning the agency and biometric data. unfortunately, there is less positive news on asylum. despite the important efforts of the italian presidency, which resulted in substantial progress in these difficult negotiations, it was not possible to reach agreement on the directive on minimum procedural standards or to break the deadlock already created at the end of the greek presidency on the other directive on refugee status and subsidiary protection. the european council can only reaffirm the political importance of this matter and invite the council to reach an agreement at least before the fifth anniversary of the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, on 1 may. in the context of the union's migration policy, the european council will also deal with the fundamental issue of the reception and integration of legal immigrants, in particular the importance of promoting interreligious dialogue as a factor of social cohesion, a theme to which the italian presidency devoted a conference of interior ministers on 30 and 31 october. migration policy cannot be effective without genuine and active collaboration with third countries which are the origin of these flows or through which they pass, a collaboration which will have to be developed in a spirit of constructive partnership. in this context, it is appropriate to highlight the positive interinstitutional agreement between parliament, the council and the commission, which should be formalised in the coming days, on the establishment of a programme of technical and financial assistance to third countries in the field of asylum, and the launch of a monitoring and evaluation mechanism for these countries in the fight against illegal immigration, as requested by the thessaloniki european council. finally, in the context of judicial cooperation in criminal matters, the european council will express its satisfaction at the agreement reached following the tenacious mediation work of the italian presidency on the framework decision on the fight against drug trafficking, a major concern of european public opinion. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the next european council in brussels will take place a few months before the accession treaty enters into force. the heads of state or government will be called upon to provide important indications as regards the completion of the enlargement process, in particular in the light of the reports presented by the commission on 5 november. as regards the countries in the process of accession - as you know - the council already expressed its views on 17 november on the commission's follow-up reports on their state of preparation for accession. in particular, the foreign ministers noted with satisfaction the high level of alignment achieved by the acceding countries in the various areas of the acquis, and we therefore expect the heads of state or government to confirm these positive considerations. the enlargement to take place in 2004 is therefore increasingly looking like a success and thus confirms the correctness of the decisions taken by the heads of state or government in copenhagen last december. of course, as was to be expected, given the great effort required of the acceding countries, there are areas of the acquis where the preparation process is not yet complete, areas where our future partners must therefore be invited to make the necessary efforts. the recent commission strategy paper shows unequivocally that bulgaria and romania have made considerable progress towards joining the union. these countries are now ready to take the decisive steps leading to their accession. the european council therefore has a responsibility to facilitate these steps by giving them a sufficiently precise path. this also applies to deadlines, in particular those relating to the conclusion of accession negotiations, the signing of the treaty and, finally, their entry into the union. these are, of course, steps whose implementation depends mainly on the governments of bulgaria and romania. however, in order to encourage this commitment, the heads of state or government will, in the view of the presidency, have to give clear indications on the stages of this future path, which will therefore have to be in line with the timetables: 2004 for the conclusion of the negotiations; 2005 for the signature of the accession treaties and 2007 for accession to the european union. the european council will also have to provide indications on the timetable for defining the financial framework for the accession of bulgaria and romania, welcoming in particular the commission's wish to present it before the end of january, following the criteria for allocating resources already adopted in the past for the accession countries. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think that each of us in this chamber has reason to be pleased with the considerable efforts made by turkey in terms of institutional reforms, as well as with its further progress towards meeting the copenhagen political criteria. appropriate recognition of these positive developments should therefore be fully reflected in the european council conclusions. we must also make sure that we give turkey our suggestions and encouragement to continue along this path, and also highlight the areas where ankara is asked to make a particularly strong commitment. the medium-term objective remains that of adequately preparing turkey for the decision to be adopted by the european council within one year. finally, with regard to cyprus, the presidency believes that the heads of state or government should reiterate the call already made to the parties to reach a concerted solution before their accession date, while recalling that a solution to the cyprus question would significantly promote turkey's aspirations to join the european union. as always, the european council will devote due attention to the union's external relations and to the main topics of international concern. i shall not dwell on this aspect because, particularly as regards the crisis areas, we are awaiting the latest developments on the ground. i also believe that we cannot avoid discussing issues such as the situation of the middle east peace process, the situation in iraq and the developments in the critical dialogue with iran. the debate on the security strategy, which began last june, will also conclude at the european council with the adoption of an excellent document setting out the problems for the security of the union and how to deal with them. this is to guide the operational decisions of governments and to increase public awareness and support for the increased commitment to security now needed across the union. the heads of state or government will also be invited to examine the progress report on esdp in order to give the future presidency a detailed mandate on the subject. acquiring more capabilities remains our first commitment. the european council will therefore welcome with particular emphasis the decision to create a european agency specifically committed to the development and acquisition of new military capabilities. in conclusion, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to remind you that the next european council will be called upon to adopt the first multiannual strategic programme which will guide the council's activities over the next three years. first, we need strong policies and stronger coordination at european level to promote economic growth, job creation and social protection. secondly, we must provide a common response to the international challenges of security, freedom and justice. thirdly, we must join forces to meet our responsibilities on the world stage and to promote our values and interests. these are the progress has been made towards the adoption of a procedure for amending the constitutional elements relating to european policies. the commission will support any effort by the presidency in this direction. in view of the new challenges that will have to be met, the constitution cannot and must not become a brake on our future action. as regards the work of the convention, the only progress european capacity to put economic governance at the service of the growth strategy. some countries even propose the reintroduction of the right of veto where the convention has abolished it, for example in trade policy. we are therefore clearly faced with two options: either a divided europe that is merely a spectator on the world political stage, or a united europe that contributes to peace, growth and sustainable development. europe, faced with the choice between these two opposite options, risks becoming a marginal continent on a global scale, surrounded by powerful protagonists. the draft constitution, in its present form, provides the instruments through which a united europe could act more effectively. nothing less, but nothing more. it does not create a political project for the future. the central question for national leaders in the igc is therefore not whether they are committed to an ambitious european project. the real question is whether they will collectively find the strength to adopt the instruments necessary for any european project. the convention has preserved and improved the balance of power between the institutions of the european union. a strong commission is essential to ensure the impartial application of european rules, and the commission's powers in key areas such as the control of state aid should not be reduced at the last minute. our aspiration to become a genuine union of peoples and states is expressed in the proposed system of double majority voting for council decisions. democratic legitimacy is enhanced by the strengthening of the legislative, political and budgetary powers of the european parliament, and the power of the court of justice to uphold the rule of law has been partially strengthened. one thing is clear, ladies and gentlemen: the commission will oppose until the last minute of the intergovernmental conference any attempt to reduce the powers of the european parliament, especially in the budgetary field. (applause) how can the european parliament and the commission be expected to explain and defend a constitution which the parliament itself has rejected? no explanation would hold up. the commission notes with satisfaction that the presidency has recognised that a system of cohabitation between commissioners with and without voting rights would be too complex and, above all, would not work. there is a simple solution, which preserves equality between the commissioners, namely a commission composed of one commissioner per member state, with a more decentralised decision-making structure and a system of checks and balances guaranteeing full collegiate status. this is the solution which the commission would like to see enshrined in the constitution. finally, the double majority voting system proposed by the convention - 50% of the member states representing at least 60% of the union's population - is simple and fair. any changes should facilitate decision-making within the college. the mr president, i should like to address a theme raised by the president-in-office of the council which nobody else has yet spoken about but which, for more than one person in this house, is of great moment and significance. the president-in-office mentioned that the question is being raised as to whether the minimum number of meps per state is too low. is it wrong to retain a relatively low basic membership in a new and enlarging union? let us pause and reflect upon this. at the moment, in britain which is composed of three nations, england, scotland and wales wales is currently represented in this house by five members. after the new constitution comes into effect, if it does, the number of members representing wales in this house will drop to four. malta will have five. i do not object at all to malta having five members: it is a fine thing for small countries to have proper representation. as a scot, how could i think otherwise? we must not forget, however, that the principle of degressive proportionality has a deep justification. degressive proportionality says that every state in this union must be represented in this house by a sufficient number of meps so as fully to express the political diversity of that state. rightly, therefore, even the 400 000 citizens of malta should have at least five members, but perhaps no more. if you insist, rightly, on keeping a maximum ceiling of membership, the upshot of increasing yet further the degressive proportionality threshold above five will be to cut the representation of significant parts of existing member states. in the debates we had about the competences of the union, mr lamassoure reminded the house of the importance of partner regions, countries like flanders, galicia, euskadi and, indeed, scotland. these are significant parts in the union. if you cut their representation you deny them the degressive proportionality on which you rightly insist for countries such as malta or cyprus. do not do that. this is not a trivial point. at the convention, as a member representing scotland, i tried many times to alert colleagues to the significance of entrenching certain aspects of the common fisheries policy that are unacceptable to us. i was not heeded. the upshot of that is that it will be impossible for me, as a strong supporter of this idea of a european constitution, to persuade my political colleagues in scotland to back ratification of the text because i now know that on that point it will not be changed. my appeal was neglected. had i been representing a larger force i might have been heard. what a pity! do not neglect degressive proportionality for the components of the states of the union in insisting on it for the states.
mr president, the british conservatives i.e. the european democrats do not support the idea that the proposed european union constitution as discussed currently at the igc in rome is merely a tidying-up exercise. we believe it significantly alters the balance of power between member states and the european union institutions. we believe it is one more stage in the process of setting up a federal super-state with its flag, currency, army and now constitution, rather than a simplifying treaty basing itself on a unique supranational creation between sovereign member states. we are concerned at the new, high-profile role of the council president and the proposed foreign minister and eu legal personality, which will enhance the perception that the eu is a de facto state and will shortly be demanding membership of the un security council. we are opposed to the passerelle clauses which jeopardise our veto rights over taxation, social security and, most worryingly, cfsp, which includes security and defence. theoretically, it becomes possible for a new british government to be out-voted over the deployment of its own troops already committed by a previous administration. we have also seen concessions over a separate planning headquarters for autonomous eu operations, which will play into the hands of isolationist us strands who will be happy to see europeans go it alone as they question the need to keep the us tied into nato, an organisation which in my view has served us well for so long. we reject the charter of fundamental rights - mr president, it is quite clear from discussions that everyone wants to finish in december. the problem is that everyone wants to make their concessions at the last possible minute - and preferably not at all. so there is a danger that despite a general willingness to conclude at the december european council, we end up, as in nice, with it going on long into the night with last-minute deals cobbled together. there is a danger that no agreement will be reached at all. at the moment, member states to a degree are still posturing. they are taking rigid and firm positions even though they know they will have to compromise if they want to succeed in december: therein lies the biggest danger facing the intergovernmental conference. i am convinced that a reasonable, acceptable deal can be found on the bulk of the points, but there is one that seems to be extraordinarily difficult: the system of voting in the council. the convention wrestled with the age-old problem of whether we want equality of states or equality of citizens. it came up with the novel and balanced solution of the double majority, with one vote every state counts equally, and with the other vote states are weighted according to their population: absolute equality of citizens. what could be fairer? poland, spain and some other countries, however, are insisting on returning to the opaque nice formula, which is neither very fair nor very logical. i regret this, and i hope that they will shift their position. i know too from discussions - notably with polish colleagues - how difficult the national context in poland is and how this has regrettably become a cause célèbre, notably for opposition parties - poland has a minority government. but how can we compromise, how can we find a way out between two radically different solutions? speaking purely personally, and off the top of my head, may i invite the italian presidency to look at what happened in the early 1990s, before enlargement to sweden, finland and austria? there was then a big row in the council about adapting the qualified majority system, then it was about the threshold: what threshold is needed to obtain a qualified majority and what is a blocking minority? at the time, one state - regrettably and shamefully my own, the united kingdom - refused to change the system. it wanted to keep the same blocking minority in an enlarged union, which would have made decision-taking even more difficult. there was deadlock. what happened, in your own country mr president? at ioannina, a compromise was reached the so-called 'ioannina compromise' whereby the union switched to the new system, but a declaration was adopted saying that in the future, states that were in the minority, but which would not have been outvoted under the old system could, if they wished, then object to the decision and insist that discussions continue. in practice, that clause was never used but it enabled face to be saved at the time, it enabled the transition to the new system and perhaps something along those lines is the only way forward on this very difficult point of the double majority. perhaps we should switch to the new system, but with a declaration allowing states perhaps for a transitional period to invoke the old system if they found themselves in the minority. i am sure they would not do this very often, but it would allow them now to save face and go home with an acceptable solution.
mr president, i very much support the joint resolution which my group has signed up to in relation to the summit and the social forum. the important thing is that once again it seeks to strike the essential balance that was established at lisbon: the balanced policy mix combining economic, social and employment policies in an overall framework of sustainable development. i hope governments will not succumb to the temptation to try in any way to skew that policy mix at the forthcoming summit. there is one element in the resolution that causes me some concern: the second part of paragraph 10. my group will request a separate vote on that point and many will be voting against it. why would that be? mr president, the obituaries for the stability pact have been written before and then held back as the patient lurched on, if only on life support. what we witnessed last week was finance ministers giving the last rites to rules which were intended to guarantee the long-term stability of our currency and economy. of course, the guilty parties deny all responsibility, or claim 'the pact is dead, long live the pact'. but the truth is that the eurozone's two leading economies have sent a message to all the small countries in the eurozone, and to the acceding countries, which reads 'do as we say, not as we do'. and i should like to point out to mr tremonti that the italian presidency has failed in its duty by acting as an associate in the endeavours of the countries concerned to flout the pact, rather than ensuring that the rules were respected. we will pay a heavy price for the cavalier disregard of finance ministers for the rules of the stability pact. we will pay a price in terms of damage to the trust between member states, in terms of lost credibility in the eyes of our citizens, and, in the long run, in terms of higher interest rates, lower growth and currency instability. unless our leaders agree on a revised and workable framework for fiscal stability, and inscribe this in our basic law, then we are left with nothing but a broken gentlemen's agreement. countries which gave up their currencies on the understanding that they would not be expected to pay for the debts of their neighbours have a right to demand more than that. that is why my group welcomes the stand agreed interpretation of a set of rules to prevent a borrowing free-for-all. liberal democrats believe that a well-run economy and a stable currency require taxes and spending to be in balance over the socialist group in this house agree with us is matched only by my delight at his conversion. the revised rules should provide sticks and carrots to ensure that we take advantage of periods of economic growth to run budgets in balance or in surplus and reduce national debt. countries which operate a responsible policy in the good times could benefit from more flexibility in bad times to let borrowing take the strain. these rules should provide for early action against countries which do not control their deficits in periods of growth, to force them to take corrective measures. a new target for the underlying budget balance could be added, and government expenditure on investment should also be taken into account. the european commission should have greater authority to police these new rules, since national governments have shown that they cannot be trusted to do so. this has been a bad week for the rule of law in the european union. my group hopes that at the summit in brussels our leaders will recognise their responsibility to salvage, from the wreckage of the stability pact, some credibility for europe's fiscal policy . mr president, i should like to make some constructive points about how to get out of the present mess. the first is that there must be a sense of shared responsibility. remember that the problem for both germany and france began because of the budget relaxations, the tax cuts and public spending increases introduced between 1999 and 2002. in each country that budget easing amounted to more than 1.5% of gdp. if it had not happened, both countries would today be within the 3% limit. yet no institution, neither the commission nor the european central bank, nor any member of this house, warned those governments against such easing. the system failed and we are all duty-bound to put it right. this is important, too, because the stability and growth pact is not a judicial procedure, but a political procedure that relies on the support of the finance ministers for recommendations and, ultimately, sanctions. ministers and the commission must have a common understanding of how the pact should be applied. there should be a clear code of conduct on the interpretation of the pact so that it can be credible for the future. there must be a reinforcement of discipline in the good years and, in the short term, there must be an agreement on the size and speed of the adjustments necessary for the countries in breach to move back to balance. the pact itself recognises that it will not always be possible to remedy excessive deficits immediately if there are special circumstances. those special circumstances should now be defined to include the risk of a further prolongation of the recession in germany and in france which, together, represent half of the euro area. it is not in anyone's interest to prolong the recession, nor is it in anyone's interest to undermine the credibility of the pact. the law must be respected. with goodwill and imagination this circle can be squared. we urge the commission and the finance ministers to do so. madam president, i want to raise the case of a british man on death row in ohio in the united states. kenny richey was convicted 16 years ago of arson and the murder of a two-year old girl who died in the fire. but new forensic evidence presented six years ago may well establish his innocence. however, he remains on death row and could be given an execution date any time. this is because us law provides that no new evidence can be introduced after a certain stage. the prosecutor has said: 'even though this new evidence may establish mr richey's innocence, the ohio and united states constitution nonetheless allows him to be executed because the prosecution did not know that the scientific testimony offered at the trial was false and unreliable.' so they know his conviction is unsafe, but he could still be executed. that accounts for why amnesty international has called it one of the most compelling cases of innocence human rights campaigners have ever seen. madam president, i will be circulating an e-mail petition and would urge all colleagues to support it, either to have the case reviewed in the light of the new evidence, or, as a last resort, to appeal for clemency.
rapporteur. – mr president, my report is on the proposal for tripartite contracts and agreements between the european authorities and the member states, and local and regional authorities. this is, one might think, rather a mouthful for what is essentially a simple idea. the point is, as the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy pointed out in its opinion on this matter, much of the implementation of important aspects of european policy environmental policy, regional policy and other policies, including transport is carried out in member states at a level of government below that of the centralised state government. and yet there is a danger of inadequate connection between the commission, at the centre, and local and regional government. any steps that can be taken to improve these connections are greatly to be welcomed and much to be encouraged. the commission's proposal on tripartite contracts and agreements is a proposal for precisely such an improvement, and therefore my group strongly welcomes it. the committee on constitutional affairs, the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, and the environment committee also welcome it and wish to carry it forward. one of the first pilot arrangements in terms of a tripartite agreement was among cities. it was based on the idea of a sustainable city for example birmingham, stockholm and other cities in the union. it was about trying to figure out ways to make sustainability make sense. one of the interesting facts i discovered in reading a report on that pilot project was that the city of birmingham could write to the central government in london and go for weeks or months without receiving a reply. central governments in member states are often very bad at maintaining adequate contact with local and city authorities and with city regions. if we are going to make progress in implementing policies in europe, it is obvious that we must make sure there is interaction between central government, local government and government at the european level. it is important to stress and i address in particular my friend and opponent mr bradbourn on this point that this suggestion for tripartite contracts and agreements is not only a suggestion about regional government of which i know mr bradbourn disapproves it is also a suggestion about local government, of which i rather think he and his party strongly approve. we must ensure that there is real contact and connectivity and that we get things moving. sometimes in this house we use the word 'region' in a very misleading sense. for example, scotland, the constituency which i represent, is for some purposes called a region. but most of the inhabitants of scotland think it is a nation within a multinational state. and scotland itself has extremely varied regions. only yesterday i was visiting the south of scotland partnership, who were discussing some of the particular problems facing the rural south of scotland, which is very different linguistically, culturally, socially and agriculturally from central scotland and from highland scotland. they raised with me the problem of the town - the old borough. nowadays it is very difficult to sustain small towns. cities and regions have great identity but towns, in our local government system, have lost that. the sustainable city is currently being trialled as a pilot project. what about the sustainable town? we must look at governance in europe at many levels: the region, the locality, and entities which are lower than the locality in terms of current governmental structures. all these things matter. the report adopted by the constitutional affairs committee needs to be amended, not in such a way as to break the spirit of what was agreed in that committee, but in a way that completes that spirit by building in some of the points agreed on by the environment committee, all of the points agreed on by the legal affairs committee, and some of the things which have emerged from the pilot projects under way. i strongly commend the report in its amended form to the house, and i very much hope that it will be carried in the vote tomorrow.
